children.text: Calumpit Church is the Diocesan Shrine and Parish of Saint John the Baptist in the town of Calumpit, Bulacan. An Augustinian church known as Bulacan's first parish, founded in 1572, it is bound up with the painful history of the 1899 Battle of Calumpit.

The official name of Calumpit Church is the Diocesan Shrine and Parish of Saint John the Baptist, also called San Juan Bautista Parish Church. It stands in Poblacion, Calumpit, Bulacan, and belongs to the Vicariate of Saint James the Apostle in the Diocese of Malolos. There is a record that its original name was the church of Saint Nicholas of Tolentine, and the convent is said to have been called "La Casa de San Juan Bautista" by the end of 1576. Wikipedia describes it as the first Augustinian evangelization site in northern Luzon. It is smaller than the churches of Hagonoy and Malolos.

Its history goes back to May 3, 1572. There is a record that the Second Provincial Chapter of the Augustinians established Calumpit as a parish together with Lubao and Betis, and on May 3, 2022 the Diocese of Malolos held a Mass marking its 450th anniversary. The convent is known to have been established on December 28, 1575, with Candaba and Macabebe as its visitas. Afterwards, Malolos became a separate convent in 1580 and Hagonoy in 1581. However, the founding year is given differently by different sources, so it is safest to understand it as "an early Bulacan parish founded by the Augustinians in the 16th century."

The present building is believed to date from the mid-17th century, and the designer and builder are not clearly recorded. Some sources name Father Diego Vivar Ordóñez as its builder. In the 19th century the convent was damaged by erosion where rivers merge, and in 1829 Father Antonio Llanos rebuilt the bell tower. During the Philippine Revolution in 1899 fire destroyed the entire church complex, and it has come down to the present after several renovations, including an extended facade. In 2019 a historical marker of the National Historical Commission of the Philippines (NHCP) was installed.

This guide is for history and church travelers who tour Bulacan heritage sites such as Malolos and Barasoain Church and want to include Calumpit. Calumpit was also the site of the Battle of Calumpit in April 1899 during the Philippine–American War, so combining a church visit with war sites enriches the story. The church is still a place where worshippers attend Mass, so it is better to check Mass times, funerals and event schedules before you visit. The Battle of Calumpit took place on April 25–27, 1899, as American forces under Arthur MacArthur advanced north. Filipino forces destroyed the bridge over the Pampanga River and resisted, but American troops led by Frederick Funston crossed the river using a rope ferry and rafts. While Antonio Luna was away in Guagua, Gregorio del Pilar took charge of the defense and is said to have cut the iron girders of the Bagbag railway bridge so that a train could not pass. Since the church burned in the same year as this battle, the building itself can be called a witness to that era.

The facade has four round columns with Corinthian capitals, floral and scroll ornament, and reliefs depicting the lives of saints on the lowest tier. The main doorway is a trefoil arch, with a circular window in the middle and rectangular windows on both sides. In place of the earlier swaying pediment, it now has a simple triangular roofline. The architectural style is classed as early Baroque and is described as mixed with Mannerist ornament. The building is made of brick and mortar, so its aged texture remains.

A four-tiered bell tower stands to the right of the church. The old tower was criticized as low and poorly proportioned, and there is a record that Father Llanos rebuilt it in 1829. From below the tower you can see the entire facade at a glance.

blocks.title: Wooden doors telling the story of Saint John the Baptist

children.text: A wooden door carved with scenes from the life of Saint John the Baptist has recently been installed at the church's main entrance. Take time to read the carvings in front of the door. This door is a new element from the renovations, so comparing it with the old appearance is interesting.

blocks.title: Visitation relief at the side entrance

children.text: The side entrance has pink reliefs of the Visitation, the Virgin Mary visiting Elizabeth, and figures of Zechariah and Elizabeth. Unlike the facade it is quiet, so it is good for photos.

Inside are a transept, nave and narthex, with a Calvary tableau and frescoes. There is a wooden ceiling, a choir loft and a clerestory, and the dome depicts the Assumption, the Four Evangelists and Saint Lorenzo Ruiz. It is smaller than the churches of Hagonoy and Malolos, so it is easy to take in slowly. Reading the dome paintings one by one while looking up is a pleasure, and the view of the nave from the choir loft is also impressive.

blocks.title: The story of the underground tunnel

children.text: The Bulacan provincial tourism introduction says that a tunnel inside the church was used to hide gold, religious statues and jewelry during Spanish rule, and that revolutionaries and Spanish soldiers were buried there during the war. It also mentions a tradition that this was the last battlefield of General Tanaka of the Japanese Imperial Army. All of this is unconfirmed lore, so listen to it only as stories.

blocks.title: Connecting to Battle of Calumpit sites

children.text: The Battle of Calumpit on April 25–27, 1899 ended in an American victory, and Filipino forces resisted by destroying the railway bridge over the Pampanga River. Related monuments, such as the Bagbag railway bridge centennial marker, are known to be in town, so you can look for them together. Casualty figures differ greatly between sources: according to Wikipedia, Luna's telegram gives about 700 Americans and about 200 Filipinos killed, while the American official record gives 22 dead and 127 wounded (the American total of 149 matches other sources, but the Filipino toll is hard to pin down).

children.text: Travel from Manila to Calumpit via NLEX or by bus.
Look around the facade and bell tower from the plaza in front of the church.
Go inside when no Mass is on and view the ceiling paintings and dome.
Walk the side entrance and surroundings of the church and look at the NHCP marker.
Have lunch at a restaurant in town.
Look for battle-related monuments such as the Bagbag railway bridge.
Continue toward Malolos or Pulilan to carry on your itinerary.
Entry to the church may be restricted when Mass or events are on. Cover your shoulders and knees.
Visit Calumpit Church first.
Move to Pulilan and look around the town and church.
Have lunch.
Visit Malolos Cathedral and Barasoain Church.
Return to Manila around sunset.
The distances are long, so a private or chartered vehicle is efficient.
Take a bus to Calumpit or Malolos from a northern Manila terminal and get off in Calumpit town.
Bus companies and routes may change, so check current information at the terminal.
In town, you can get to the church by tricycle.
Travel time and fares vary with traffic, so confirm them locally.
From Manila, take NLEX north and use the exit toward Calumpit.
The roads around the church are narrow, so use a nearby open lot or a parking area in town.
If you use a chartered taxi or Grab, agree in advance on the round-trip waiting cost.
You can reach Calumpit by jeepney or tricycle from Malolos, Apalit and Hagonoy.
You can also arrive by jeepney from the Apalit and Hagonoy directions, so ask locally about routes.
The dry season (November–May) is more comfortable for travel. The inside of the church is relatively cool even at midday.

On the parish feast day and during Holy Week (the week before Easter), events and worshippers are many and visits may be restricted. The feast of Saint John the Baptist is around June 24, so check the diocesan announcements for the schedule. In the rainy season, low-lying areas of Calumpit sometimes flood.

On weekday daytimes there is no Mass, so you can see the interior quietly. On Sundays and feast days there are several Masses in the morning, so you can look at the exterior first and go back inside in the afternoon. Check the Mass schedule on the parish notice board or its Facebook page.

In Calumpit town there are local restaurants and snack shops that are good for a simple meal. Bulacan is close to the Pampanga River, so freshwater fish and rice dishes are common, but well-known businesses change names often, so check locally. You can buy drinks and snacks at stores near the church. If you eat around the plaza in front of the church or at restaurants near the market, you save travel time, and on hot days many visitors rest with a cold drink, ice cream or halo-halo.

Most people base their stay in Malolos, Apalit or central Manila. Calumpit does not have many large lodgings, so planning it as a day trip is easier. The church alone takes a little over an hour, so a one-day plan that also covers Malolos and Pulilan is the most efficient.
Check Mass times and event schedules with the diocese or parish announcements before you visit.
Wear clothes that cover your shoulders and knees.
Refrain from taking photos or moving around inside during Mass.
The NHCP marker can be found around the church, so read the historical text.
Combined with Malolos Cathedral and Barasoain Church, it makes a Bulacan church circuit.
Avoid the shadeless midday and visit in the early morning.
In the rainy season, check road flooding conditions in advance.
To see the ceiling paintings inside the church, it is better to tilt your head back slowly rather than squint, so sit and rest while you look.
The church is still a place of worship where Mass is held, so postpone your visit during events and funerals and observe dress and manners.
The underground tunnel and Japanese army traditions are unconfirmed, so do not treat them as fact.
In the rainy season parts of Calumpit may flood, so check road conditions before you travel.
Roads in town are narrow and busy, so watch for vehicles when walking.
Bus and tricycle fares change by season, so confirm them locally.
The founding year differs between sources as 1572, 1575 and 1779, so do not assert an exact year and understand it as "founded in the 16th century."
The cathedral of a city steeped in the history of the First Philippine Republic, easy to see together by driving.
A historic site where the First Republic constitution was drafted in 1899.
